extracted_supporting_text: Type 1 diabetes is a disease in which your pancreas does not make insulin... Managing type 1 diabetes requires keeping your blood glucose levels in target range through insulin, diet, and exercise.
claim_summary: Type 1 diabetes nutrition requires coordinating insulin, diet, and physical activity.

extracted_supporting_text: Because carbohydrates turn into glucose in the body, they have the greatest impact on blood sugar. Counting carbs helps people with type 1 diabetes match their insulin dose to the food they eat.
claim_summary: Type 1 diabetics must count carbs to determine insulin bolus doses.

extracted_supporting_text: For type 1 diabetes, eating at the same times each day is important, especially if you take certain types of insulin. Skipping meals while on insulin increases risk of hypoglycemia.
claim_summary: Meal timing consistency is critical in type 1 diabetes to prevent hypoglycemia.

extracted_supporting_text: Taking mealtime insulin before eating helps match the action of the insulin with the glucose entering the blood from food, typically 15 to 30 minutes prior to meals.
claim_summary: Coordinating mealtime insulin injection 15-30 minutes before eating is required in type 1 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Physical activity can lower blood glucose levels, sometimes up to 24 hours after exercise. Check blood sugar before exercising and carry fast-acting carbohydrates.
claim_summary: Type 1 diabetics must monitor glucose and carry fast-acting carbs during physical activity.

extracted_supporting_text: Hypoglycemia symptoms include shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, dizziness, and hunger. It is defined as blood sugar under 70 mg/dL.
claim_summary: Recognizing hypoglycemia symptoms and using fast-acting carbs is vital in type 1 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: High blood sugar can lead to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in type 1 diabetes. Symptoms include dry mouth, extreme thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath, and nausea.
claim_summary: High blood sugar and DKA warning signs in type 1 diabetes require urgent testing and clinical care.

extracted_supporting_text: Decisions regarding insulin dosing, therapy changes, or regimen adjustments must be made by qualified healthcare professionals.
claim_summary: Insulin dosing changes in type 1 diabetes must be directed by a clinician.

extracted_supporting_text: Urgent medical help is required for DKA symptoms like rapid deep breathing, vomiting, confusion, or severe unresponsive hypoglycemia.
claim_summary: Urgent emergency medical care is needed for DKA and severe hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: For type 2 diabetes, dietary patterns should promote insulin sensitivity and weight management. Prioritize non-starchy vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins.
claim_summary: Type 2 diabetes nutrition focuses on insulin sensitivity and blood glucose management.

extracted_supporting_text: Quality of carbs is key for type 2 diabetes. Choose complex, fiber-rich carbohydrates over refined grains and simple sugars to slow glucose absorption.
claim_summary: Type 2 diabetics should choose complex carbohydrates over refined grains.

extracted_supporting_text: The Plate Method is a simple visual guide: half non-starchy vegetables, one-quarter lean protein, and one-quarter carbohydrate foods.
claim_summary: The Diabetes Plate Method is a simple portion control tool for type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid sugar-sweetened beverages like soda, sweet tea, and fruit juices. Opt for water or unsweetened drinks to manage calories and blood sugar.
claim_summary: Type 2 diabetics must avoid sugary drinks and prioritize calorie-free beverages.

extracted_supporting_text: Fiber in vegetables, whole grains, and legumes slows digestion, preventing blood sugar spikes, and supports weight control by enhancing satiety.
claim_summary: Fiber-rich foods help manage blood glucose and support weight loss in type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Exercise makes cells more sensitive to insulin. Aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity.
claim_summary: Regular physical activity improves insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes; goal is 150 mins/week.

extracted_supporting_text: Losing 5% to 10% of body weight improves blood sugar control, reduces medication needs, and lowers cardiovascular risks in type 2 diabetes.
claim_summary: Losing 5-10% of body weight improves glycemic control and reduces comorbidities in type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Self-monitoring of blood glucose helps individuals see how diet and exercise affect their levels, facilitating lifestyle adjustments and clinical management.
claim_summary: Self-monitoring of blood glucose supports lifestyle modification in type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Hypoglycemia is a risk for type 2 diabetics taking sulfonylureas or insulin. Those managing with metformin or diet alone are at lower risk.
claim_summary: Hypoglycemia risk in type 2 diabetes is primary for those on sulfonylureas or insulin.

extracted_supporting_text: Working with a registered dietitian or certified diabetes educator helps personalize meal planning, taking into account medications, lifestyle, and comorbidities.
claim_summary: Type 2 diabetics should consult dietitians for personalized nutrition plans.

extracted_supporting_text: General diabetes education emphasizes balanced healthy eating, prioritizing non-starchy vegetables and minimizing refined sugars, applicable to all types.
claim_summary: General diabetes education targets basic healthy eating parameters without assuming type.

extracted_supporting_text: Diabetes recommendations differ by type; type 1 requires daily insulin injection to survive, while type 2 may be managed with diet, exercise, and oral meds.
claim_summary: Diabetes guidelines differ significantly between type 1 (insulin-dependent) and type 2.

extracted_supporting_text: Accurate identification of type 1 vs type 2 diabetes is critical for determining correct therapy, monitoring schedules, and safety support rules.
claim_summary: Patients with unspecified diabetes should confirm their diagnosis type with a healthcare provider.

extracted_supporting_text: When diabetes type is unspecified, avoid insulin dosing assumptions. Stick to general lifestyle advice like low salt, low sugar, and high fiber.
claim_summary: General diabetes advice must avoid insulin assumptions and focus on basic diet rules.

extracted_supporting_text: Prediabetes is a serious health condition where blood sugar levels are higher than normal, but not high enough yet to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.
claim_summary: Prediabetes represents a warning window where blood sugar is elevated but not yet at type 2 level.

extracted_supporting_text: Managing portion sizes of carbohydrates like rice is necessary in prediabetes, but complete elimination is not recommended. Focus on portions and quality.
claim_summary: Prediabetics should control carbohydrate portions rather than completely eliminating them.

extracted_supporting_text: Sugar-sweetened beverages add empty calories and sugar. Prediabetics should replace soda, sweet teas, and juices with water to prevent weight gain.
claim_summary: Prediabetics should avoid sugar-sweetened beverages and replace them with water.

extracted_supporting_text: Losing 5% to 7% of your body weight can cut your risk of developing type 2 diabetes by more than half for people with prediabetes.
claim_summary: Losing 5-7% of body weight dramatically cuts the risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Get at least 150 minutes per week of moderate physical activity, such as brisk walking, to help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes.
claim_summary: 150 minutes per week of moderate exercise is recommended to delay or prevent type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Structured lifestyle change programs like the National DPP help participants make lasting changes, such as eating healthier, adding activity, and managing stress.
claim_summary: Structured lifestyle modification programs support sustained prevention of type 2 diabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Prediabetes often has no symptoms. Periodic blood tests like HbA1c every 6 to 12 months are necessary to track status and progression risk.
claim_summary: Prediabetics require periodic lab screening (HbA1c) due to the asymptomatic nature of the condition.

extracted_supporting_text: Not all individuals with prediabetes require medication. Dosing or medication initiation decisions must be individualized by a physician; lifestyle changes remain primary.
claim_summary: Metformin or medication use in prediabetes is not universal; lifestyle change is the primary recommendation.

extracted_supporting_text: The American Heart Association recommends an ideal limit of no more than 1500 mg of sodium per day for most adults, especially those with high blood pressure.
claim_summary: Hypertensive adults should target a daily sodium limit of under 1500 mg.

extracted_supporting_text: Condiments like soy sauce, fish sauce, and salad dressings are high in sodium. A single tablespoon can contain a substantial portion of the daily sodium allowance.
claim_summary: Traditional condiments like fish sauce are highly concentrated sodium sources requiring moderation.

extracted_supporting_text: Most of the sodium in the diet comes from processed and restaurant foods. Reading nutrition labels helps identify hidden sodium in canned goods, deli meats, and packaged meals.
claim_summary: Processed foods are major contributors to high sodium intake; label reading is necessary.

extracted_supporting_text: Eating a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy can lower blood pressure. Potassium-rich foods help counter the effects of sodium, provided kidney function is normal.
claim_summary: Fruits and vegetables (potassium-rich) lower blood pressure, except when kidney disease is present.

extracted_supporting_text: Losing weight is one of the most effective lifestyle changes for controlling blood pressure. Every kilogram lost reduces blood pressure by approximately 1 mmHg.
claim_summary: Weight reduction directly correlates with blood pressure decreases.

extracted_supporting_text: Regular physical activity of moderate intensity, like 30 minutes of walking 5 days a week, helps lower blood pressure and manage weight.
claim_summary: 30 minutes of moderate exercise 5 days a week lowers blood pressure in hypertensive individuals.

extracted_supporting_text: Home blood pressure monitoring provides useful data for managing hypertension. Measure at consistent times and log results for physician review.
claim_summary: Regular home blood pressure monitoring supports hypertension management.

extracted_supporting_text: Antihypertensive medication plans must not be modified without direct clinical evaluation. Silent hypertension risks require continuous medication adherence.
claim_summary: Adherence to prescribed blood pressure medications is required; changes must be clinical.

extracted_supporting_text: A hypertensive crisis is defined as BP over 180/120 mmHg accompanied by symptoms like severe headache, chest pain, vision changes, or numbness. Seek immediate emergency care.
claim_summary: A hypertensive crisis (BP >180/120 mmHg with severe symptoms) requires emergency medical services.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD Stage G1 is defined by eGFR >= 90 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating normal or high kidney function, in the presence of markers of kidney damage.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G1 is characterized by normal/high eGFR (>=90) with kidney damage evidence.

extracted_supporting_text: An eGFR of >= 90 mL/min/1.73 m2 alone does not establish CKD stage G1. Other markers of kidney damage (e.g. albuminuria, hematuria, structural abnormalities) must be present for >3 months.
claim_summary: CKD G1 requires markers of kidney damage (like albuminuria) present for >3 months, not just eGFR >=90.

extracted_supporting_text: Patients with CKD G1 should be monitored at least annually with eGFR and albuminuria (UACR) measurement to assess progression risk.
claim_summary: CKD G1 patients require annual monitoring of eGFR and UACR.

extracted_supporting_text: For early stages (1-2), severe dietary restrictions of protein, potassium, or phosphorus are generally unnecessary unless recommended by a physician for specific complications.
claim_summary: Unnecessary severe dietary restrictions should be avoided in early CKD Stage G1.

extracted_supporting_text: Identify the underlying cause of CKD in stage G1 patients to optimize targeted treatment and prevent decline. Professional nephrology consultation is advised.
claim_summary: Identifying the primary cause of CKD G1 via nephrologist review is critical to guide treatment.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD Stage G2 is defined by eGFR of 60-89 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating mildly decreased kidney function, in the presence of markers of kidney damage.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G2 is defined by mildly decreased eGFR (60-89) alongside kidney damage evidence.

extracted_supporting_text: An eGFR of 60-89 mL/min/1.73 m2 without accompanying markers of kidney damage does not fulfill criteria for CKD stage G2.
claim_summary: CKD G2 diagnosis requires kidney damage markers (e.g. protein in urine) in addition to eGFR 60-89.

extracted_supporting_text: Monitor CKD G2 progression with annual measurements. Progression is defined as a sustained decline in eGFR of >5 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year.
claim_summary: Annual monitoring of eGFR is required in CKD G2 to detect rapid progression (>5 mL/min decline/year).

extracted_supporting_text: For patients with CKD and hypertension, target a systolic blood pressure of <120 mmHg when tolerated. Manage diabetes to protect residual kidney function.
claim_summary: Hypertension control (systolic <120 mmHg) and diabetes control protect kidney function in CKD G2.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid nephrotoxic agents like nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) in early stages of kidney disease to prevent sudden deterioration.
claim_summary: NSAID avoidance is crucial in CKD Stage G2 to prevent nephrotoxic injury.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD Stage G3a is defined by eGFR of 45-59 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating mildly to moderately decreased kidney function.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G3a is characterized by mildly to moderately decreased eGFR (45-59).

extracted_supporting_text: In adults with CKD G3-G5 non-dialysis, suggest a protein intake of 0.6-0.8 g/kg body weight/day to delay progression, unless contraindicated.
claim_summary: Non-dialysis CKD G3a protein target is a moderate 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day.

extracted_supporting_text: We recommend a sodium intake of <2.0 g/d (equivalent to <5 g/d of salt) in adults with CKD G3a.
claim_summary: Daily sodium intake for CKD G3a should be limited to <2000 mg (<5g salt).

extracted_supporting_text: In CKD stage G3a, potassium restriction should not be applied universally. It should be guided by serum potassium measurements rather than stage alone.
claim_summary: Potassium restriction in CKD G3a should be based on laboratory measurements, not stage alone.

extracted_supporting_text: For CKD G3a, limit inorganic phosphorus additives found in processed foods and sodas, as they are highly absorbed compared to organic phosphorus.
claim_summary: CKD G3a patients should limit inorganic phosphorus food additives.

extracted_supporting_text: In patients with CKD stage G3a with comorbid diabetes or hypertension, strict risk factor modification is required to reduce kidney decline.
claim_summary: Glycemic and blood pressure optimization preserves kidney function in CKD G3a comorbid patients.

extracted_supporting_text: Evaluate eGFR and albuminuria at least twice a year in patients with CKD stage G3a to monitor progression.
claim_summary: CKD G3a patients require laboratory monitoring of kidney function at least twice annually.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD Stage G3b is defined by eGFR of 30-44 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating moderately to severely decreased kidney function.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G3b is characterized by moderately to severely decreased eGFR (30-44).

extracted_supporting_text: In adults with CKD G3b non-dialysis, suggest a protein intake of 0.6-0.8 g/kg body weight/day to delay progression and manage uremia.
claim_summary: Non-dialysis CKD G3b protein target is restricted to 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day.

extracted_supporting_text: We recommend a sodium intake of <2.0 g/d in adults with CKD G3b to prevent fluid overload and control hypertension.
claim_summary: CKD G3b patients must restrict sodium to <2000 mg/day to avoid fluid retention.

extracted_supporting_text: For CKD stage G3b, dietary potassium restriction should be tailored based on serum potassium levels to avoid hyperkalemia complications.
claim_summary: Potassium intake in CKD G3b must be adjusted according to serum potassium laboratory results.

extracted_supporting_text: For CKD G3b, limit phosphorus rich foods (dairy, nuts, egg yolks) to maintain blood phosphorus levels and protect bone health.
claim_summary: CKD G3b patients should limit dietary phosphorus to prevent renal osteodystrophy.

extracted_supporting_text: Patients with CKD stage G3b require monitoring of eGFR and albuminuria at least three times a year to track complications.
claim_summary: CKD G3b patients require clinical and lab monitoring at least three times annually.

extracted_supporting_text: Referral to a registered dietitian specializing in kidney disease (renal dietitian) is highly recommended at stage G3b to prevent malnutrition while restricting nutrients.
claim_summary: CKD G3b patients should consult a renal dietitian for specialized nutrition planning.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD Stage G4 is defined by eGFR of 15-29 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating severely decreased kidney function.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G4 is characterized by severely decreased eGFR (15-29).

extracted_supporting_text: Suggest a protein intake of 0.6 g/kg/d in adults with CKD G4 who are not on dialysis to reduce uremic toxins and delay renal replacement therapy.
claim_summary: Non-dialysis CKD G4 patients require strict protein restriction to 0.6 g/kg/day.

extracted_supporting_text: We recommend a sodium intake of <2.0 g/d in adults with CKD G4 to prevent volume overload and cardiac complications.
claim_summary: CKD G4 patients must limit sodium to <2000 mg/day to prevent cardiovascular overload.

extracted_supporting_text: Hyperkalemia is common and dangerous in CKD stage G4. Dietary potassium restriction is critical when blood levels rise, and must be monitored closely.
claim_summary: CKD G4 patients require strict dietary potassium restriction when hyperkalemia is present.

extracted_supporting_text: In CKD stage G4, limit phosphorus to 800-1000 mg/day. Avoid dairy, nuts, and foods containing phosphate additives to protect arteries.
claim_summary: CKD G4 patients must limit phosphorus to 800-1000 mg/day.

extracted_supporting_text: Fluid intake in CKD stage G4 must be carefully monitored. Restriction is typically required only when there is signs of fluid retention or decreased urine output.
claim_summary: Fluid restrictions in CKD G4 must be individualized based on fluid retention or urine output.

extracted_supporting_text: Prepare stage G4 patients for renal replacement therapy (RRT), educating them on hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and transplantation options.
claim_summary: CKD G4 patients should receive education and counseling on renal replacement therapy options.

extracted_supporting_text: Refer patients in CKD stage G4 to specialist multidisciplinary teams (nephrologists, dietitians) to manage severe renal complications and nutrition.
claim_summary: CKD G4 patients require multidisciplinary nephrology team referral.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD Stage G5 is defined by eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2, indicating kidney failure. The non-dialysis subgroup requires active conservative care.
claim_summary: CKD G5 non-dialysis is characterized by eGFR < 15 without active renal replacement therapy.

extracted_supporting_text: Suggest a protein intake of 0.6 g/kg/d in adults with CKD G5 non-dialysis to delay dialysis. This is contrast to dialysis patients who require protein loading.
claim_summary: Protein intake for CKD G5 non-dialysis must be restricted to 0.6 g/kg/day, unlike dialysis patients.

extracted_supporting_text: We recommend a sodium intake of <2.0 g/d in adults with CKD G5 non-dialysis to control fluid volume and hypertension.
claim_summary: Sodium restriction to <2000 mg/day is mandatory in CKD G5 non-dialysis.

extracted_supporting_text: Hyperkalemia is common and dangerous in CKD stage G5 non-dialysis. Restrict dietary potassium strictly and monitor serum levels regularly to avoid cardiac arrest.
claim_summary: Strict potassium restriction is required in CKD G5 non-dialysis due to life-threatening hyperkalemia risk.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit phosphorus to 800 mg/d in CKD G5. Use prescribed phosphate binders with meals to manage hyperphosphatemia.
claim_summary: Phosphorus restriction to 800 mg/day and phosphate binders are recommended in CKD G5 non-dialysis.

extracted_supporting_text: In stage G5 non-dialysis, fluid intake should match urine output plus 500 mL to prevent fluid overload and heart failure.
claim_summary: Fluid intake in CKD G5 non-dialysis should be limited to urine output plus 500 mL.

extracted_supporting_text: Close clinical monitoring is required in CKD stage G5 non-dialysis to identify uremic symptoms requiring initiation of renal replacement therapy.
claim_summary: CKD G5 non-dialysis requires close clinical supervision to detect uremic complications.

extracted_supporting_text: Emergency medical attention is required for stage G5 non-dialysis patients presenting with severe shortness of breath, inability to breathe lying down, or signs of hyperkalemia.
claim_summary: Fluid overload or severe hyperkalemia in CKD G5 non-dialysis require immediate emergency care.

extracted_supporting_text: Nutritional needs for dialysis patients change significantly from pre-dialysis stages. The goal is replacing nutrients lost during dialysis sessions.
claim_summary: Nutrition for dialysis patients differs significantly from non-dialysis CKD.

extracted_supporting_text: Dialysis removes protein waste but also amino acids. Dialysis patients require a high protein intake of 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day to maintain nutritional status.
claim_summary: Dialysis patients require a high protein diet (1.0-1.2 g/kg/day) to prevent muscle wasting.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit sodium to <2000 mg/d in dialysis. Excess sodium causes thirst, leading to excessive interdialytic weight gain (fluid overload) between sessions.
claim_summary: Sodium restriction under 2000 mg/day is required in dialysis to control fluid gain.

extracted_supporting_text: Potassium guidelines in dialysis vary by modality. Peritoneal dialysis removes more potassium than hemodialysis, often requiring less restriction or even supplementation.
claim_summary: Potassium guidelines for dialysis patients depend on modality (hemodialysis vs peritoneal) and lab values.

extracted_supporting_text: Dialysis does not clear phosphorus efficiently. Limit intake to 800-1000 mg/d and take prescribed phosphate binders with meals.
claim_summary: Dialysis patients require phosphorus limits (800-1000 mg) and phosphate binders with meals.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit fluid intake between hemodialysis sessions to ensure interdialytic weight gain stays below 3% to 5% of dry body weight.
claim_summary: Hemodialysis patients must limit fluid intake to keep interdialytic weight gain below 3-5% of dry weight.

extracted_supporting_text: Collaborate closely with the dialysis care team to adjust diet, fluid, and binder usage based on monthly clinical lab evaluations.
claim_summary: Dialysis patients should coordinate care with their dialysis clinic team.

extracted_supporting_text: General healthy diet for unspecified kidney disease focuses on lowering sodium intake and avoiding processed foods.
claim_summary: General kidney education emphasizes lower sodium and avoiding processed foods.

extracted_supporting_text: Nutrient limits differ dramatically between non-dialysis CKD stages (protein restriction) and dialysis stages (protein loading). Stage must be identified.
claim_summary: CKD nutritional rules differ dramatically by stage and dialysis status.

extracted_supporting_text: Providing accurate eGFR or doctor's staging diagnosis is necessary to receive stage-appropriate nutritional guidance.
claim_summary: CKD patients should provide stage/eGFR data to receive safe recommendations.

extracted_supporting_text: When stage is unknown, avoid specific potassium, phosphorus, or fluid restrictions to prevent adverse nutritional outcomes.
claim_summary: Unspecified CKD guidance should avoid specific stage-related restrictions.

extracted_supporting_text: High uric acid levels (hyperuricemia) do not mean you have gout. Gout is diagnosed only when uric acid crystals form in joints, causing acute inflammation.
claim_summary: Asymptomatic hyperuricemia is a risk factor, but does not constitute a gout diagnosis.

extracted_supporting_text: Uric acid is made when the body breaks down purines in food. Limiting purine-rich foods helps prevent uric acid crystals from depositing in joints.
claim_summary: Purine restriction reduces uric acid production and joint deposition in gout.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid organ meats like liver, kidneys, and sweetbreads because they contain very high levels of purines and can trigger acute gout attacks.
claim_summary: Organ meats are extremely high purine foods that gout patients must avoid.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit red meats like beef, pork, and lamb. Moderate intake is advised, replacing them with lean poultry or plant proteins.
claim_summary: Gout patients should moderate red meat consumption.

extracted_supporting_text: Certain seafoods (sardines, herring, anchovies, shellfish) are high in purines. Gout patients should limit their intake to prevent flares.
claim_summary: High-purine seafoods like shellfish and sardines must be limited by gout patients.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid alcohol, especially beer, because it contains high purines and decreases the kidneys' ability to excrete uric acid, triggering attacks.
claim_summary: Alcohol (especially beer) impairs uric acid excretion and triggers gout attacks.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid foods and beverages sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup, as fructose metabolism stimulates purine production and raises uric acid.
claim_summary: Fructose-sweetened foods and drinks stimulate purine production and should be avoided in gout.

extracted_supporting_text: Drink plenty of water (8-16 cups a day) to help flush uric acid from your body and prevent kidney stones.
claim_summary: Adequate hydration (2-2.5L/day) aids uric acid excretion and prevents kidney stones.

extracted_supporting_text: During a gout flare, restrict purines strictly and rest the affected joint. Chronic management allows a moderately restricted, balanced diet.
claim_summary: Diet during acute gout flares is strictly restrictive compared to chronic management.

extracted_supporting_text: Dietary changes help but do not replace medications designed to lower uric acid levels (like allopurinol). Medication adherence is critical.
claim_summary: Dietary modifications do not replace pharmacotherapy (uric acid lowering drugs) in gout.

extracted_supporting_text: Sustainable weight management is about a lifestyle that includes healthy eating, physical activity, and behavior changes, rather than short-term diets.
claim_summary: Obesity management focuses on sustainable lifestyle modifications rather than quick-fix diets.

claim_summary: Portion control techniques aid calorie management for obesity.

claim_summary: Lower energy density foods support weight loss by promoting fullness with fewer calories.

extracted_supporting_text: Sugar-sweetened beverages contribute a lot of empty calories. Eliminating them is a simple way to create a calorie deficit.
claim_summary: Eliminating sugar-sweetened beverages is a key step to establish a calorie deficit for weight loss.

extracted_supporting_text: Physical activity is crucial for weight loss maintenance. Combined with diet, aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly to sustain weight loss.
claim_summary: Physical activity (150 mins/week) is critical for weight loss maintenance in obesity.

claim_summary: Extreme/fad diets are unsafe and ineffective for sustainable obesity management.

claim_summary: Obesity management in older adults must prioritize muscle retention to prevent frailty.

extracted_supporting_text: Perform at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, spread over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 consecutive days without exercise.
claim_summary: Type 2 diabetics should engage in 150 minutes/week of aerobic activity spread over at least 3 days.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit sodium to under 2300 mg/day, or 1500 mg/day if hypertension is present, to mitigate cardiovascular risks in type 2 diabetes.
claim_summary: Sodium restriction to under 2300 mg/day is recommended for type 2 diabetes management.

extracted_supporting_text: When diabetes type is unknown, emphasize safe general dietary guidelines like non-starchy vegetables, and avoid specific carb-insulin adjustments.
claim_summary: Unspecified diabetes guidance should focus on general healthy eating and avoid specific therapeutic rules.

extracted_supporting_text: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune beta cell destruction (absolute insulin lack); type 2 is insulin resistance. Type specification is essential for safety.
claim_summary: Autoimmune nature of type 1 diabetes vs lifestyle factors of type 2 dictates therapeutic differences.

extracted_supporting_text: Medication initiation or dosage adjustments are contraindicated without clinical diagnostic typing. Consultation with a provider is mandatory.
claim_summary: Medication changes are contraindicated for patients with unspecified diabetes classification.

extracted_supporting_text: Liquid sugars like milk tea and soda cause rapid glucose spikes and worsen insulin resistance. Substitute with water or unsweetened tea.
claim_summary: Prediabetics should eliminate sugar-sweetened beverages to improve insulin response.

extracted_supporting_text: A short 10-15 minute walk immediately after meals helps muscles absorb glucose, flattening postprandial blood sugar spikes.
claim_summary: Postprandial light walking assists immediate glucose clearance in prediabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Sleep restriction alters hunger hormones and raises cortisol levels, worsening insulin resistance and weight control.
claim_summary: Adequate sleep (7-8 hours) is necessary to maintain normal insulin sensitivity in prediabetes.

extracted_supporting_text: Do not eliminate carbohydrates completely. Extreme carb cutting is unsustainable and causes muscle loss. Focus on complex carbohydrates and portions.
claim_summary: Prediabetics should focus on carbohydrate quality and moderation rather than total elimination.

extracted_supporting_text: Progression risk is higher for sedentary individuals, overweight, family history of diabetes, or age >=45. Regular testing is required.
claim_summary: High-risk prediabetic populations require proactive screening and lifestyle change.

extracted_supporting_text: Measure HbA1c every 6 to 12 months to monitor long-term average glucose and evaluate lifestyle intervention efficacy.
claim_summary: HbA1c monitoring every 6-12 months tracks prediabetes progression and management.

extracted_supporting_text: Structured programs offer guidance on weight loss, dietary modifications, and physical activity to prevent type 2 diabetes.
claim_summary: Structured lifestyle intervention programs support sustained prediabetes reversal.

extracted_supporting_text: Condiments like soy sauce are high in sodium, with a single tablespoon containing a substantial portion of the daily sodium allowance.
claim_summary: Soy sauce is a concentrated sodium source that hypertensive patients should restrict.

extracted_supporting_text: Instant noodles and their seasoning packets contain high amounts of sodium, often exceeding recommended daily limits in a single serving.
claim_summary: Instant noodles contain high sodium levels; seasoning packets must be restricted.

extracted_supporting_text: Processed meats like sausages and deli meats contain high levels of sodium added during processing. Fresh meats are preferred.
claim_summary: Processed meats are rich in sodium and should be minimized by hypertensive individuals.

extracted_supporting_text: Check sodium content on nutrition facts labels. A %DV of 5% or less is low in sodium, while 20% or more is high.
claim_summary: Hypertensive patients should select packaged foods with a %DV of sodium under 5%.

extracted_supporting_text: The DASH eating plan is rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy. It restricts saturated fat and sodium to 1500-2300 mg.
claim_summary: The DASH eating plan is clinically proven to reduce blood pressure; limits sodium to 1500-2300 mg.

extracted_supporting_text: Caffeine causes a temporary increase in blood pressure by blocking vasodilating hormones. Uncontrolled hypertensive patients should avoid high intake.
claim_summary: Caffeine causes transient blood pressure elevations; restrict when BP is uncontrolled.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit alcohol to prevent rise in blood pressure. Recommendations are max 2 drinks/day for men and 1 drink/day for women.
claim_summary: Alcohol restriction to under 2 drinks/day (men) and 1 drink/day (women) protects blood pressure.

extracted_supporting_text: Aerobic exercise for 30-45 minutes, 5 days a week, lowers systolic blood pressure by 5-8 mmHg over time.
claim_summary: Regular aerobic exercise reduces systolic blood pressure by 5-8 mmHg.

extracted_supporting_text: For accurate home blood pressure readings, sit quietly for 5 minutes, arm at heart level, feet flat on the floor, no caffeine or tobacco prior.
claim_summary: Proper sitting posture and relaxation are required for accurate home blood pressure measurement.

extracted_supporting_text: In patients with CKD and diabetes, optimization of glycemic control (glycemic target) is required to reduce progression risk in early stage G1.
claim_summary: Glycemic control targets protect the kidneys from microvascular damage in early stage G1 CKD.

extracted_supporting_text: Hyperlipidemia in CKD stage G1 increases atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis and cardiovascular risks. Saturated fat restriction is advised.
claim_summary: Saturated fat restriction mitigates cardiovascular risks in CKD Stage G1.

extracted_supporting_text: At CKD stage G1, drink adequate fluids (1.5-2 liters) to aid waste excretion unless contraindicated by cardiac conditions.
claim_summary: Adequate hydration is encouraged in early CKD stage G1 to support renal clearance.

extracted_supporting_text: In patients with CKD stage G2 and hypertension, ACE inhibitors or ARBs are recommended as first-line agents due to renal protective effects.
claim_summary: First-line ACEi/ARB therapy provides renal protection in CKD Stage G2 with hypertension.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid herbal supplements and unprescribed traditional medicines in CKD stage G2 to prevent direct renal tubular toxicity.
claim_summary: Unprescribed herbal supplements are contraindicated in CKD Stage G2 to prevent renal toxicity.

extracted_supporting_text: Recommend regular physical activity (minimum 150 minutes/week) in patients with CKD stage G2 to lower cardiovascular risk factors.
claim_summary: Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health in CKD Stage G2.

extracted_supporting_text: In adults with CKD G3a non-dialysis, suggest a protein intake of 0.6-0.8 g/kg body weight/day from high-quality sources to mitigate uremic load.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G3a protein target is a moderate 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day.

extracted_supporting_text: Limit inorganic phosphorus additives in CKD G3a; they are highly absorbed and contribute to hyperphosphatemia and vascular calcification.
claim_summary: Inorganic phosphorus food additives should be restricted in CKD Stage G3a.

extracted_supporting_text: Anemia screening (hemoglobin levels) is recommended annually in CKD stage G3a due to potential decline in erythropoietin production.
claim_summary: CKD Stage G3a patients require annual anemia screening.

extracted_supporting_text: Iodinated contrast media poses a nephrotoxic risk in CKD stage G3a. Coordinate with a nephrologist and ensure adequate hydration.
claim_summary: Iodinated contrast media use requires prior clinical preparation in CKD Stage G3a.

extracted_supporting_text: Protein restriction (0.6-0.8 g/kg/d) and substitution with plant-based protein is suggested in CKD stage G3b to prevent metabolic acidosis.
claim_summary: Plant-based protein substitution is recommended within the CKD Stage G3b target of 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day.

extracted_supporting_text: In CKD stage G3b, adjust dietary potassium when serum levels exceed 5.0 mEq/L to prevent cardiac arrhythmia risks.
claim_summary: Potassium dietary restriction is indicated in CKD Stage G3b when serum levels exceed 5.0 mEq/L.

extracted_supporting_text: Monitor serum calcium and phosphorus in CKD stage G3b to evaluate renal bone disease risk and calcium-phosphate product elevations.
claim_summary: Calcium and phosphorus laboratory monitoring is required in CKD Stage G3b to prevent bone disease.

extracted_supporting_text: Renally cleared medications require dosage adjustments in CKD stage G3b (e.g. metformin dosage limits) to prevent drug accumulation toxicity.
claim_summary: Renally cleared medications require clinical dosage review in CKD Stage G3b.

extracted_supporting_text: In patients with CKD stage G4 and metabolic acidosis, oral sodium bicarbonate therapy is suggested to slow decline and manage bone loss.
claim_summary: Metabolic acidosis management via bicarbonate is indicated in CKD Stage G4.

extracted_supporting_text: Immunize patients in CKD stage G4 against hepatitis B early, as antibody response is better prior to starting hemodialysis.
claim_summary: Hepatitis B immunization is recommended in CKD Stage G4 prior to dialysis initiation.

extracted_supporting_text: Preserve peripheral veins in the non-dominant arm of patients in CKD stage G4 to protect future arteriovenous fistula (AVF) surgical sites.
claim_summary: Peripheral vein preservation is required in CKD Stage G4 for future dialysis access.

extracted_supporting_text: Hyperkalemia is critical in CKD stage G4. Avoid salt substitutes containing potassium chloride, and monitor dietary potassium strictly.
claim_summary: Salt substitutes containing potassium chloride are contraindicated in CKD Stage G4 due to hyperkalemia risk.

extracted_supporting_text: CKD-MBD is highly prevalent at stage G4. Calcitriol or phosphate binder dosing must be carefully controlled; avoid high-dose calcium without clinical review.
claim_summary: High-dose calcium supplements are contraindicated in CKD Stage G4 without clinician monitoring.

extracted_supporting_text: In CKD stage G5 non-dialysis, treat metabolic acidosis to maintain serum bicarbonate above 22 mEq/L to delay ESRD decline.
claim_summary: Target serum bicarbonate level in CKD G5 non-dialysis is above 22 mEq/L.

extracted_supporting_text: Phosphate binders must be taken with meals in CKD stage G5 to bind dietary phosphorus and prevent hyperphosphatemia complications.
claim_summary: Phosphate binders must be taken concurrently with meals in CKD Stage G5 non-dialysis.

extracted_supporting_text: Plant-based phosphorus is less absorbed (30-40% absorption rate) in CKD stage G5 non-dialysis due to phytate binding, making it safer than animal phosphorus.
claim_summary: Plant-based phosphorus has a low absorption rate (30-40%) in CKD Stage G5 non-dialysis.

extracted_supporting_text: Uremic symptoms like anorexia and nausea in CKD stage G5 non-dialysis indicate close need for dialysis transition planning.
claim_summary: Uremic symptoms in CKD G5 non-dialysis indicate the need for dialysis transition planning.

extracted_supporting_text: Stop metformin in CKD stage G5 (eGFR < 15) to prevent lactic acidosis. Dosing of other oral antidiabetics must be clinically reviewed.
claim_summary: Metformin is contraindicated in CKD Stage G5 non-dialysis due to lactic acidosis risk.

extracted_supporting_text: Hemodialysis fluid limits target interdialytic weight gain below 3% to 5% of dry weight. Limit fluid to urine output plus 500-700 mL.
claim_summary: Fluid limits in hemodialysis target interdialytic weight gain below 3-5% of dry body weight.

extracted_supporting_text: Peritoneal dialysis allows more liberal fluid and potassium intake than hemodialysis because fluid removal is continuous.
claim_summary: Peritoneal dialysis patients generally have less restrictive fluid and potassium limits than hemodialysis patients.

extracted_supporting_text: Adjust dietary potassium in hemodialysis based on monthly serum potassium to avoid hyperkalemia and hypokalemia.
claim_summary: Hemodialysis dietary potassium adjustment must be guided by monthly serum potassium results.

extracted_supporting_text: Peritoneal dialysis removes significant proteins (5-15g/day). A high protein diet of 1.2 g/kg/day is required.
claim_summary: Peritoneal dialysis patients require a high protein intake (1.2 g/kg/day) to compensate for dialysis losses.

extracted_supporting_text: Protect the AVF access site in hemodialysis patients: avoid BP checks or infusions on the access arm to prevent stenosis.
claim_summary: Hemodialysis patients must protect their vascular access (AVF) by avoiding blood pressure measurement on the access arm.

extracted_supporting_text: Water-soluble vitamins are lost during hemodialysis. Supplement with specialized renal vitamins containing B-complex and C.
claim_summary: Water-soluble vitamins are cleared during hemodialysis and require supplementation.

extracted_supporting_text: Avoid specific fluid and protein targets when CKD stage is unknown. Maintain basic low-sodium diet and seek eGFR testing.
claim_summary: Dietary guidelines for unspecified CKD should focus on general sodium limits without setting fluid or protein targets.

extracted_supporting_text: Serum creatinine alone is not sufficient to evaluate renal function. Staging requires calculated eGFR and urine albumin levels.
claim_summary: CKD evaluation requires calculated eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR).

extracted_supporting_text: NSAID avoidance is crucial for all CKD stages, especially when stage is unspecified, to prevent precipitating acute-on-chronic kidney injury.
claim_summary: NSAID medications are contraindicated for patients with unspecified chronic kidney disease.

extracted_supporting_text: Meat extracts and gravies contain highly concentrated purines and should be avoided by gout patients.
claim_summary: Meat broths and extracts are concentrated purine sources that gout patients should avoid.

extracted_supporting_text: Purine-rich vegetables (beans, lentils, spinach, asparagus) do not increase gout flare risk like animal purines do.
claim_summary: Purine-rich vegetables do not associate with increased risk of gout flares.

extracted_supporting_text: Low-fat dairy products can lower uric acid levels and help prevent gout attacks by promoting renal clearance.
claim_summary: Low-fat dairy products promote uric acid excretion and help manage gout.

extracted_supporting_text: Rapid weight loss or fasting triggers gout attacks because ketone bodies compete with uric acid excretion in the kidneys.
claim_summary: Rapid weight loss or fasting is contraindicated in gout due to ketone-induced hyperuricemia.

extracted_supporting_text: In CKD, decreased uric acid clearance raises gout risk; conversely, urate crystals in the kidneys can accelerate renal damage.
claim_summary: Gout and CKD have a bidirectional exacerbating relationship.

extracted_supporting_text: Target uric acid is less than 6.0 mg/dL (or 5.0 mg/dL for severe gout) to dissolve existing crystals and prevent flares.
claim_summary: Long-term uric acid target for gout control is under 6.0 mg/dL.

extracted_supporting_text: Spirits and strong alcohols increase lactic acid, which competes with uric acid excretion, causing rapid spikes in blood levels.
claim_summary: Distilled spirits impair uric acid clearance via lactic acid accumulation.

extracted_supporting_text: Dietary modifications reduce uric acid by only 1-2 mg/dL. They support but do not replace uric-acid-lowering medications.
claim_summary: Dietary changes reduce uric acid by a modest 1-2 mg/dL, necessitating medical therapy for chronic gout.

extracted_supporting_text: Emotional eating in response to stress or anxiety is a major factor in calorie surplus. Identify and substitute with non-food stressors.
claim_summary: Emotional eating triggers calorie surplus and requires behavioral modification.

extracted_supporting_text: Sleep deprivation alters leptin and ghrelin levels, increasing appetite and abdominal fat storage via elevated cortisol.
claim_summary: Sleep restriction promotes appetite and fat accumulation via leptin/ghrelin and cortisol disruption.

extracted_supporting_text: Eat low energy density foods (vegetables, water-rich foods) first to promote satiety and naturally reduce intake of high-calorie foods.
claim_summary: Pre-loading with low energy density foods supports portion control and weight loss.

extracted_supporting_text: High-protein intake increases satiety due to high thermic effect of food and helps preserve lean muscle mass during calorie restriction.
claim_summary: Dietary protein supports weight loss by increasing satiety and preserving muscle mass.

extracted_supporting_text: A safe and sustainable rate of weight loss is 1 to 2 pounds (0.5 to 1 kg) per week to prevent yoyo weight gain and muscle loss.
claim_summary: Safe, sustainable weight loss rate is 0.5 to 1.0 kg per week.

extracted_supporting_text: Regular physical activity (150 minutes/week) and resistance exercises prevent weight regain by maintaining basal metabolic rate.
claim_summary: Regular physical activity (150 mins/week) is critical to prevent weight regain after loss.

extracted_supporting_text: Abdominal fat increases insulin resistance. Losing 5-10% of body weight improves insulin action and glycemic control in type 2 diabetes.
claim_summary: Visceral fat drives insulin resistance; weight reduction of 5-10% restores glycemic control.

extracted_supporting_text: Weight loss reduces cardiac workload and blood volume. Every kg of weight lost decreases systolic blood pressure by approximately 1 mmHg.
claim_summary: Weight loss directly reduces systolic blood pressure by approximately 1 mmHg per kg lost.

extracted_supporting_text: Sarcopenic obesity in older adults carries high risk of frailty. Restrictive diets must be combined with high protein and resistance exercise.
claim_summary: Restrictive diets in older adults must preserve muscle via high protein and resistance exercise to avoid frailty.

extracted_supporting_text: Eating disorders (anorexia, bulimia, binge eating) require specialized psychiatric and clinical nutrition support, excluding automatic advice.
claim_summary: Eating disorders exclude individuals from automated self-guided weight loss recommendations.

extracted_supporting_text: Insufficient or contradictory clinical values require retesting and professional diagnostic review before setting nutritional limits.
claim_summary: Contradictory or incomplete clinical data requires clinical recheck and excludes automated advice.

extracted_supporting_text: Patients with complex comorbidities (e.g. advanced CKD G4 with obesity) have conflicting nutrient needs and must be excluded from automated RAG guidance.
claim_summary: Automated recommendations are disabled for patients with conflicting comorbidities; clinician referral is mandatory.
